unit.title: Manage personal stress in the workplace

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is stress?
options: A kind of illness that only managers get
A sign that a person is lazy or weak
Something that only happens at home, never at work
The body and mind's reaction to pressure or demands

questions.stem: Which statement about stress is true?
options: All stress is harmful and must be avoided completely
Some pressure helps, but too much for too long is harmful
Stress only affects people who are not good at their jobs
Stress cannot affect the body, only the mind

questions.stem: Which of these is a common physical sign of stress?
options: Headaches, tight muscles and trouble sleeping
Better sleep and more energy than usual
A steady heartbeat and relaxed shoulders
Feeling calm and hungry at regular times

questions.stem: Which is a common behaviour sign that a co-worker may be under too much stress?
options: Arriving on time every day and joking with the team as usual
Taking normal breaks and eating lunch with others
Snapping at people, making mistakes and missing work
Keeping their tools clean and their area tidy

questions.stem: Which of these is an emotional sign of stress?
options: Feeling cheerful, rested and relaxed for most of the working day
Looking forward to coming to work
Feeling anxious, irritable or low most of the time
Feeling proud after finishing a good weld

questions.stem: Which of these is a common cause of stress at work?
options: Too much work and deadlines that cannot be met
Clear instructions and a fair workload
A supervisor who listens and gives support
Regular breaks and enough rest time between each shift

questions.stem: In a hot, noisy fabrication workshop, which conditions can add to a worker's stress?
options: Good ventilation and cool drinking water
Heat, constant noise and poor lighting
Clean, well-lit work areas with fans
Ear protection that fits and works well

questions.stem: Which of these is a cause of stress outside work that can still affect a person at work?
options: Getting enough sleep every night
Spending time with supportive friends
Taking part in a hobby they enjoy
Money worries or family problems

questions.stem: Why can stress be dangerous in a welding and fabrication workshop?
options: Stress makes the welding machine use more power
A stressed worker may lose focus and have an accident
Stress makes steel harder to cut and grind
Stressed workers always work more slowly and safely

questions.stem: If high stress goes on for a long time, what can it lead to?
options: Health problems such as high blood pressure and depression
Stronger muscles and better eyesight
A longer life and fewer illnesses
No effects at all, because the body soon gets fully used to it

questions.stem: What is "burnout"?
options: A burn injury from hot metal or spatter
A fault in a welding machine that has been left to overheat
Running out of welding gas in the middle of a job
Feeling worn out and drained after long-term stress

questions.stem: What is a stress diary used for?
options: Writing down the hours you have worked so that you are paid
Keeping a list of your co-workers' mistakes
Noting what stressed you, when, and how you reacted
Planning holidays for the whole year

questions.stem: Which of these is a healthy way to cope with stress?
options: Regular exercise, such as walking or playing football
Drinking more alcohol after work to relax
Smoking more cigarettes during breaks
Staying up very late every night scrolling on your phone

questions.stem: Why does getting enough sleep help you manage stress?
options: It means you can skip breakfast and lunch
A rested body and mind cope better with pressure
It stops you from ever feeling any stress again at all
It means you do not need to take breaks at work

questions.stem: Working in the Jamaican heat, which simple habit helps both your health and your stress levels?
options: Drinking sweet energy drinks all through the day instead of water
Skipping lunch to finish the job sooner
Working through every break to save time
Drinking enough water and taking short breaks in the shade

questions.stem: Which is a quick relaxation method you can use during a short break?
options: Shouting at the nearest person to let off steam
Running up and down the stairs ten times
Slow, deep breathing for a few minutes
Drinking three cups of strong coffee

questions.stem: Why is using alcohol or drugs to cope with stress a bad idea?
options: They are too expensive to buy every week
They hide the problem, harm health and are unsafe at work
They make you too relaxed to enjoy your work
They only work on weekends and holidays

questions.stem: Which of these is an unhealthy way of coping with stress?
options: Cutting yourself off from friends and family
Talking to someone you trust about the problem
Going for a walk at lunchtime
Making a list of tasks in order of importance

questions.stem: How can a "to-do" list help with stress at work?
options: It means you never have to finish any task
It lets someone else do all of your work
It shows what must be done, so you can take it step by step
It replaces any need to talk to your supervisor about the work

questions.stem: You have several tasks and not enough time. What should you do first?
options: Do the easiest tasks first and leave the rest
Try to do every one of the tasks at the same time, quickly
Leave them all and hope they go away
Sort them by how urgent and important they are

questions.stem: Your supervisor asks you to take on an extra job when you already cannot finish your own work. What is the best response?
options: Explain your workload politely and agree on priorities
Say yes, then stay late every night to finish it
Refuse rudely and walk away from the supervisor
Say yes but quietly leave the job undone

questions.stem: What does it mean to be assertive?
options: Always getting your own way by shouting
Saying what you need clearly and calmly, with respect
Agreeing with everyone to avoid arguments
Keeping quiet about problems so you do not upset anyone

questions.stem: A co-worker keeps taking your tools without asking, and it is making you angry. What is the best first step?
options: Hide their tools so that they know how it feels
Shout at them loudly in front of the whole class and the instructor
Talk to them calmly in private about the problem
Ignore it and let your anger build up

questions.stem: Who could a trainee at the Centre talk to if stress is affecting their work?
options: Nobody, because stress is a private matter
Only a customer who happens to be visiting the workshop that day
Someone they do not know on social media
Their instructor, a counsellor or someone they trust

questions.stem: When should a person see a doctor or other health professional about stress?
options: Only after they have been off work for a whole year
When stress affects sleep, health or daily life for weeks
Never, as doctors do not deal with stress
Only if a co-worker tells them to go

questions.stem: A co-worker tells you they feel hopeless and are thinking of harming themselves. What should you do?
options: Take it seriously, stay with them and get help at once
Tell them to stop being silly and get back to work
Promise to keep it secret and say nothing to anyone
Tell everyone in the workshop so that they know

questions.stem: What can an employer do to reduce work stress for staff?
options: Give staff more work with shorter deadlines
Stop all breaks so that work finishes sooner
Keep any changes to the work a secret until the very last minute
Plan fair workloads, give clear instructions and listen

questions.stem: What does "work–life balance" mean?
options: Working every day of the week, including holidays
Keeping your toolbox balanced so it does not fall off the bench
Having enough time for work, rest, family and interests
Earning the same amount as everyone else

questions.stem: The Centre is changing the timetable and you feel worried about it. Which is the most helpful thing to do?
options: Stop coming to class until it changes back
Spread rumours about the change to all the other trainees in the group
Ask the instructor for the facts and how it affects you
Keep the worry to yourself and say nothing

questions.stem: You notice that a classmate seems very stressed. What is a helpful thing to do?
options: Tease them a little so that they laugh and forget all about it
Ask quietly if they are OK and listen to them
Tell the class about their problems
Avoid them until they feel better

questions.stem: Which kind of eating helps the body cope with stress?
options: Regular meals with fruit, vegetables and water
Skipping meals and eating snacks late at night
Mostly sugary drinks and fried food
One very large meal at the end of the day only

questions.stem: Why are regular short breaks important during a long welding job?
options: They are only for people who are not strong enough
They mean the job can be left unfinished
They give time to check social media
They help you rest, stay alert and avoid mistakes

questions.stem: Which way of thinking helps to reduce stress?
options: Expecting every job to go wrong
Focusing on what you can control
Blaming yourself for every problem
Comparing yourself with everyone else

questions.stem: Why is it useful to know your own early signs of stress?
options: So that you can hide them from your instructor
So that you can take time off work whenever you feel like it
So that you can blame others for your stress
So that you can act early, before stress builds up

questions.stem: What should a personal stress action plan include?
options: A list of people to blame for your stress
The dates of every public holiday and long weekend for the whole year
The things that stress you, steps to deal with them, and who can help
Only a list of foods that you dislike

questions.stem: A trainee is being bullied by another trainee, and it is causing stress. What should they do?
options: Report it to the instructor or another trusted staff member
Fight back so that the bully stops
Keep quiet and put up with it
Leave the course without telling anyone

questions.stem: How does physical activity help to reduce stress?
options: It makes you too tired to do any work
It means that you no longer need any sleep at night
It only helps if done for five hours a day
It releases tension and improves mood and sleep

questions.stem: Why does talking about a problem with someone you trust often help?
options: It means the problem is now their job to fix
It can ease the worry and help you see a way forward
It always makes the problem go away at once
It gives you something to complain about later

questions.stem: How can planning your day help to reduce stress?
options: It means you never need to talk to anyone
It means nothing unexpected can ever happen
You know what to do first and can set realistic goals
It lets you leave all the hard jobs for other people to do

questions.stem: Which is a good way to switch off from work stress at home?
options: Spend time on hobbies, family, faith or rest
Check work messages every hour until midnight
Keep going over the day's problems in your head
Argue with family about what went wrong at work

questions.stem: You have tried a new way of coping with stress for two weeks. What should you do next?
options: Give up, because it did not work on the first day
Keep on doing it forever, whether it helps you or not
Tell everyone in the group that they must all use the same method
Check whether it has helped and change your plan if needed

questions.stem: Where can you find out what support your workplace or the Centre offers for stress?
options: In the welding machine's operating manual or its warranty card
In the handbook, or from student support staff
On the back of a cement bag
From a stranger on social media

questions.stem: A welder feels exhausted and cannot concentrate. What is the safest thing to do?
options: Carry on welding but work a little faster to finish sooner
Take off their helmet to get more air
Stop, tell the supervisor and take a break
Drink an energy drink and keep working

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of "positive" pressure that can help you perform well?
options: A fair deadline that keeps you focused
Being shouted at every day by a co-worker
Working 16-hour shifts every day
Not knowing if you will have a job next week

questions.stem: Who is responsible for managing your own stress?
options: Only your doctor
Only your employer
Nobody, as it cannot be managed
You, with support from others

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters EAP stand for, in workplace support services?
Name the hormone the body releases quickly when it senses danger, to prepare it for action.
The body's automatic reaction to danger is called "fight or ___". What is the missing word?
What is the word for the things or events that cause a person stress?
Health guides say most adults need at least how many hours of sleep a night?
When setting goals, what does the "S" in SMART stand for?
Stress affects a person's physical health. What other kind of health does it affect? (Two words)
What do the letters HR stand for, as the name of a company's staff department?
Health guides commonly suggest adults do at least how many minutes of moderate exercise a week?
What is the word for losing too much water from the body, which makes you tired, irritable and less able to cope in the heat?
Name the drug found in coffee, tea and energy drinks that can make anxiety and poor sleep worse if you have too much.

Name the body system that fights off illness, which long-term stress can weaken.
What do the letters OSH stand for, in workplace safety?
What is the word for deep tiredness and lack of energy that makes it hard to concentrate and work safely?

essays.stem: Explain what workplace stress is, and describe the difference between helpful pressure and harmful stress.
essays.modelAnswer: Stress is the way the body and mind react when the demands on a person feel greater than their ability to cope. When we face pressure, the body releases hormones such as adrenaline, so the heart beats faster and the muscles get ready for action. A little pressure can be helpful. For example, a fair deadline for a welding job can keep a trainee focused, alert and working well, and the feeling passes once the job is done. This is sometimes called positive pressure. Stress becomes harmful when the pressure is too much, goes on for too long, or the person feels they have no control over it, such as a heavy workload every day, constant conflict or worry about money. Then the body stays on alert, and the person may become tired, ill, anxious or unable to concentrate. Harmful stress can lead to mistakes, accidents, poor health and burnout, so it should be noticed early and managed.
markingPoints: Stress is the body and mind's reaction when demands feel greater than the ability to cope
Describes the body's reaction (hormones, faster heart, alert)
Helpful pressure: short-term, keeps you focused, passes when the task is done, with an example
Harmful stress: too much, too long or no control, with an example
Effects of harmful stress (illness, mistakes, accidents, burnout) and the need to manage it early

essays.stem: Describe the physical, emotional and behaviour signs of stress. Give at least two examples of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Stress shows itself in the body, in feelings and in the way people act. Physical signs include headaches, tight neck and shoulder muscles, an upset stomach, a racing heart, feeling tired all the time and trouble sleeping. Some people catch colds more often because stress weakens the body's defences. Emotional signs include feeling worried or anxious, being irritable or quick to anger, feeling low or tearful, feeling overwhelmed, and losing confidence. A stressed person may also find it hard to concentrate, make decisions or remember things. Behaviour signs include snapping at co-workers, arguing, making more mistakes than usual, coming late or missing work, withdrawing from friends, eating much more or much less, and using more alcohol, cigarettes or caffeine. In a workshop, a stressed worker may rush, skip safety steps or forget PPE. Everyone shows stress in their own way, so it helps to know your own early signs and to notice changes in others.
markingPoints: At least two correct physical signs (such as headaches, tight muscles, poor sleep, upset stomach)
At least two correct emotional signs (such as anxiety, irritability, feeling low or overwhelmed)
At least two correct behaviour signs (such as snapping, mistakes, lateness, withdrawing, more alcohol)
Mentions effects on thinking or concentration
Notes that signs differ between people and links them to safety at work

essays.stem: Describe common causes of stress for workers in a welding and fabrication workshop, both at work and outside work.
essays.modelAnswer: At work, a common cause is too much work with tight deadlines, for example several gates and grills promised to customers in the same week. Unclear instructions, or not knowing what is expected, can also cause stress, as can a lack of control over how the work is done. Conflict with co-workers or a supervisor, bullying, or feeling unfairly treated adds pressure. The working conditions matter too: the heat of a Jamaican workshop, constant noise from grinders, fumes, poor lighting and long hours all make people tired and tense. Worry about safety, about making mistakes on an expensive job, or about losing work when business is slow can also be stressful. Outside work, money problems, such as bills or debt, are a major cause. Family problems, caring for children or sick relatives, relationship troubles, long or costly travel to work, poor housing and health problems can all follow a person into the workshop and affect how they cope.
markingPoints: Workload and deadlines
Unclear instructions, lack of control, conflict or bullying
Working conditions such as heat, noise, fumes and long hours
Job insecurity or fear of mistakes
Outside work: money, family, travel, housing or health problems

essays.stem: Explain why stress is a safety issue in a workshop, and describe what a worker should do if stress is affecting their concentration.
essays.modelAnswer: A welding and fabrication workshop has many hazards: arc light, hot metal, sparks, electricity, grinders, saws and heavy steel. Working safely needs full attention. A stressed worker may be tired, distracted or in a hurry, so they are more likely to skip a safety step, forget PPE, misjudge a cut, leave a hot piece unmarked or make a mistake with a machine. This can injure them or someone else and can spoil the work. Stress can also cause poor sleep and fatigue, which slow reactions. If stress is affecting their concentration, the worker should stop the task and make it safe, for example by switching off the machine. They should tell the supervisor or instructor honestly that they are not able to focus, take a short break, drink water and breathe slowly. If needed, they can ask to change to a lower-risk task for a while. If the problem keeps happening, they should talk to someone about the cause and get support.
markingPoints: Workshops have serious hazards that need full attention
Stress causes distraction, rushing, fatigue and mistakes
Links this to injury to self or others and to damaged work
Stops and makes the task safe, and tells the supervisor honestly
Takes a break, may change to a lower-risk task, and seeks support if it continues

essays.stem: Describe four healthy ways to manage stress, and explain how each one helps.
essays.modelAnswer: Regular physical activity, such as walking, football, dancing or cycling, helps because it uses up the energy that stress builds up in the body, loosens tight muscles and releases chemicals that improve mood and sleep. Getting enough sleep, usually at least seven hours for an adult, helps because a rested body and mind think more clearly and cope better with pressure. Eating regular, healthy meals and drinking enough water, especially in the heat, keeps energy steady and avoids the tiredness and irritability that come from hunger or dehydration. Talking to someone you trust, such as a friend, family member, instructor, pastor or counsellor, helps because sharing a problem can ease the worry and help you see a way forward. Other good ways include planning your work with a to-do list, taking short breaks, slow deep breathing, and making time for hobbies, faith and family. The best plan uses a few of these together, every day.
markingPoints: First healthy method with a correct explanation (for example exercise)
Second healthy method with a correct explanation (for example sleep)
Third healthy method with a correct explanation (for example healthy eating and water)
Fourth healthy method with a correct explanation (for example talking, planning, breathing, hobbies)
Notes that using several methods regularly works best

essays.stem: Explain why unhealthy ways of coping, such as alcohol, drugs, smoking or cutting yourself off from others, make stress worse.
essays.modelAnswer: Unhealthy ways of coping may seem to give quick relief, but they do not deal with the cause of the stress, and they bring new problems. Alcohol and drugs change mood for a short time, but afterwards the person often feels worse, sleeps badly and becomes more anxious or low. Using them can lead to dependence, money problems, and trouble with family and the law. In a workshop they are especially dangerous, because they slow reactions and affect judgement around machines, hot metal and electricity, and being under the influence at work can lead to accidents and losing the job. Smoking and too much caffeine raise the heart rate and harm health over time, and they can make sleep worse. Cutting yourself off from friends and family removes the support that helps people cope, so problems seem bigger and loneliness grows. Overeating or skipping meals also harms health and energy. Healthy methods are slower but they last.
markingPoints: Unhealthy methods give only short-term relief and do not deal with the cause
Alcohol and drugs: worse mood and sleep, dependence, money and family problems
Alcohol and drugs are dangerous at work: slower reactions, accidents, job loss
Smoking and caffeine harm health and sleep
Isolation removes support and makes problems seem bigger

essays.stem: Explain how good time management and setting priorities can reduce stress, using examples from a workshop job.
essays.modelAnswer: Much work stress comes from feeling that there is too much to do and not enough time. Good time management gives back a feeling of control. At the start of the day, I can write a to-do list of everything that must be done, for example finishing the welds on a gate, cutting steel for a grill and cleaning my booth. Then I sort the tasks by how urgent and how important they are, and do the most urgent and important first, such as the gate that the customer is collecting at noon. I break big jobs into smaller steps, so that I can see progress and tick them off. I estimate how long each task will take and leave some spare time for problems. I avoid distractions, such as my phone, while working. If I still cannot fit everything in, I tell my supervisor early and politely, explain my workload and agree which tasks come first. Planning like this reduces rushing, mistakes and last-minute panic.
markingPoints: Links stress to feeling there is too much to do, and time management to control
Uses a to-do list
Sorts tasks by urgency and importance, with a workshop example
Breaks jobs into steps, estimates time and avoids distractions
Tells the supervisor early and agrees priorities if work cannot fit

essays.stem: Describe how to deal calmly and assertively with a conflict with a co-worker, for example over shared tools or space.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would wait until I feel calm, rather than reacting in anger, and take a few slow breaths. Then I would ask to speak with the co-worker in private, at a good time, not in front of the class. I would explain the problem clearly and calmly, using "I" statements, for example: "I get held up when my chipping hammer goes missing, because I have to stop and look for it." I would not shout, call names or blame. Then I would listen to their side without interrupting, because there may be a reason I did not know about, such as their own tools being broken. Together we would look for a fair solution, for example labelling tools, returning them straight after use, or asking the instructor for more tools. We would agree what each of us will do. If the problem continues, or if there is bullying or a threat, I would report it to the instructor or supervisor rather than let it build up.
markingPoints: Waits until calm before speaking
Speaks in private at a suitable time
States the problem clearly and calmly with "I" statements, without blame
Listens to the other person's side
Agrees a fair solution, and reports to the supervisor if it continues or is serious

essays.stem: Describe where a trainee or worker can get help with stress, and explain when they should seek professional help.
essays.modelAnswer: Help can come from many places. At the Centre, a trainee can talk to their instructor, a guidance counsellor or student support staff, and at work a worker can talk to their supervisor or the human resources department. Some employers have an employee assistance programme, which gives free, private counselling. Outside work, family, trusted friends, a pastor or church group, or a community group can listen and support. Health professionals, such as a doctor at a health centre, a counsellor or a psychologist, can give advice and treatment. A person should seek professional help when stress lasts for weeks, when it affects their sleep, eating, health or ability to work, when they feel low or hopeless most of the time, or when they are relying on alcohol or drugs to cope. If someone has thoughts of harming themselves, they need help straight away: they should tell someone they trust, contact a doctor or go to the nearest hospital, or call the emergency services.
markingPoints: Help at the Centre or work: instructor, counsellor, supervisor, human resources, EAP
Help outside work: family, friends, pastor, community groups
Professional help: doctor, counsellor, psychologist
When to seek professional help: lasting weeks, affecting sleep, health or work, or relying on alcohol or drugs
Thoughts of self-harm need help at once: tell someone, doctor, hospital or emergency services

essays.stem: Describe how you would make and review a personal stress management action plan.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would find out what causes my stress by keeping a stress diary for one or two weeks, writing down when I felt stressed, what caused it, how I felt and what I did. From the diary I would pick my main causes, for example falling behind with practical work and money worries. For each cause I would write a SMART goal and the steps to reach it, such as planning my week with a to-do list, asking my instructor for help with welding positions, and making a simple budget. I would add healthy habits to my plan, such as walking three times a week, going to bed by a set time, drinking enough water and cutting down on energy drinks. I would write down the early signs that show my stress is rising, and who I can talk to for support. After two to four weeks, I would review the plan: check which steps helped, which did not, and change the plan where needed. I would keep reviewing it regularly.
markingPoints: Uses a stress diary to find the causes
Picks the main causes and sets SMART goals and steps for each
Includes healthy habits
Notes early warning signs and who can give support
Reviews the plan after a set time and changes it where needed

practical1.title: Make a stress-awareness poster and give a toolbox talk for the welding workshop
practical1.brief: As a group, plan, make and present a stress-awareness poster for the Centre's welding workshop, then use it to give a 10-minute toolbox talk to the assessor and another group. The poster must show: what stress is; common causes in a workshop; physical, emotional and behaviour signs; why stress is a safety risk around machines and hot work; at least four healthy ways to cope; and where trainees can get help at the Centre and outside it. Share the work so that each member researches and writes one section and presents it in the talk. Use your own words and drawings. Collect written feedback from at least two listeners on a simple feedback form, and note one change you would make. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the poster, the planning notes and the feedback forms once for the whole group.
materials: Chart paper or a large card, markers, rulers and glue
Paper and pens for planning notes
Information sheets from the instructor on stress and where to get help
photos: The group's planning notes, showing who is doing each section
The toolbox talk, with each member presenting their section
The completed feedback forms and the group's note on one change
checklist: Took part in planning and agreed their section with the group
Wrote their section in their own clear words, and it was correct
Included correct signs, causes or coping methods for their section
Linked stress to safety in the workshop where it fitted their section
Presented their section clearly and answered a question about it
Listened to others and helped collect and act on the feedback
safety: If the poster is put up in the workshop, fix it away from welding booths and hot work
Use scissors and craft knives carefully, and keep the work area tidy
Do not share any member's private or personal details on the poster
If any member is upset by the topic, they can step out and talk to the instructor

practical2.title: Role play: handling stress at work, then write a stress action plan
practical2.brief: As a group, act out three short workplace scenes given by the assessor, for example: a welder with too much work speaking to their supervisor; two co-workers in conflict over shared tools; and a worker noticing that a co-worker seems very stressed and offering support. Each member plays a part in at least one scene and observes at least one other, filling in an observation sheet on what went well and what could be better. After each scene, the group discusses it and writes down the main points. Then each member writes a stress action plan, covering causes, early signs, SMART goals and steps, healthy habits and who can give support. A member may write the plan for a made-up worker if they prefer not to share personal details. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the written sheets to the group's practical.
materials: Three scene cards from the assessor
Observation sheets, one for each member
Blank stress action plan forms, one for each member
Pens, a clipboard and a quiet room or corner of the classroom
photos: The group reading the scene cards and choosing roles
The group's notes from the discussion after the scenes
Each member's completed stress action plan (personal details covered if wanted)
checklist: Played their part in a scene clearly, staying calm, polite and assertive
Used good listening and "I" statements where the scene needed it
Suggested a sensible solution or source of help in their scene
Completed an observation sheet with useful comments
Took part in the group discussion after each scene
Completed a stress action plan with causes, signs, SMART goals, healthy habits and support
safety: Keep the role plays calm: no shouting, pushing or touching
Treat each other with respect; nobody is forced to share private matters
Any member who becomes upset can stop and speak privately with the instructor
Keep the room tidy so that nobody trips while moving between scenes
